body:
Why rated power is not constant output

A photovoltaic module is commonly described by its rated peak power, expressed in watts-peak (Wp) or kilowatts-peak (kWp). The rating identifies its output under specified standard test conditions. It does not mean the module produces that power continuously throughout the day.

Common standard test conditions for photovoltaic modules include an irradiance of 1,000 W/m2 and a cell temperature of 25°C, together with the standard AM1.5 global solar spectrum, representing a sunlight path through the atmosphere 1.5 times the vertical path. The cell temperature is important: it is not necessarily the same as the surrounding air temperature.

Actual irradiance varies throughout the day and may be below the standard test value. The operating temperature of a panel exposed to the Sun can also be considerably higher than 25°C.

Conversion efficiency

Photovoltaic conversion efficiency is the proportion of incoming solar power on the cell or module area that is converted into electrical power under the stated measurement conditions.

Suppose sunlight delivers 1,000 W of power to a solar module and the module produces 200 W of electrical power. Its conversion efficiency under those conditions is 20%.

The remaining incident energy is not all transformed into useful electricity. Losses arise from reflection, incomplete absorption, conversion limitations and heat production.

Conversion efficiency should not be confused with the fraction of a day for which electricity is generated. A 20% efficient panel does not mean it operates for only 20% of daylight hours.

From peak power to daily energy

The total electricity generated depends on both the power produced and the duration of production. The relevant distinction is between kW, a unit of power, and kWh, a unit of energy.

A useful concept is an equivalent peak-sun hour. It expresses daily solar irradiation as the number of hours that would deliver the same solar energy at an irradiance of 1,000 W/m2.

Illustrative daily generation

Consider a PV array rated at 2 kWp that receives daily irradiation equivalent to 4 peak-sun hours on its module surface.

Its ideal reference energy would be 2 kW multiplied by 4 hours, or 8 kWh.

If actual operation delivers 80% of that reference energy, daily electricity output would be 6.4 kWh. This example illustrates the calculation; it is not a guaranteed daily yield for a real installation.

Four equivalent peak-sun hours do not necessarily mean that sunlight remains exactly at peak intensity for 4 consecutive hours. Actual sunlight intensity rises and falls throughout the day.

Factors affecting photovoltaic output

  • Irradiance: With other conditions held constant, stronger usable sunlight generally increases the electrical output.
  • Temperature: For conventional crystalline-silicon modules, higher cell temperatures generally reduce conversion efficiency and available power at the same irradiance.
  • Orientation and tilt: The direction and inclination of a panel affect the amount of solar radiation reaching its surface.
  • Shading: Trees, buildings and other obstructions can reduce the output of affected modules or parts of an array.
  • Dust and soiling: Deposits on the surface can reduce the light entering solar cells.
  • System losses: The inverter and other equipment consume or lose some energy during conversion and delivery.
  • Age and condition: Module performance may gradually decline with use, and equipment faults can further reduce generation.

These factors explain why 2 solar systems with the same installed peak capacity can produce different amounts of electricity.

Efficiency, performance ratio and capacity factor

MeasureWhat it comparesMain purpose
Module efficiencyElectrical power produced with incident solar powerMeasures sunlight-to-electricity conversion at the module
Performance ratioActual system energy yield with the yield expected from received irradiation and rated capacityIndicates combined operational losses
Capacity factorActual electricity generated with the electricity possible at continuous rated power over the same periodIndicates output relative to maximum continuous rated operation

Performance ratio (PR) helps distinguish losses in an installation from variation in sunlight availability. It commonly compares actual final energy yield with a reference yield calculated from the solar irradiation reaching the array. Capacity factor, in contrast, reflects both solar resource availability and other factors affecting actual generation. Neither measure is identical to the conversion efficiency of an individual solar cell.

A sunny and hot day does not automatically provide the highest efficiency. More sunlight can increase generation, but higher cell temperature can simultaneously reduce the efficiency of silicon modules.

Prelims focus

  • Rated PV power is measured under specified test conditions, not continuously available outdoor conditions.
  • Common standard test conditions include 1,000 W/m2 irradiance and 25°C cell temperature.
  • kWp describes rated power; kWh describes electrical energy generated.
  • Higher cell temperature generally reduces crystalline-silicon PV efficiency at the same irradiance.
  • Soiling, shading, orientation and conversion losses affect actual output.
  • Trap: Module efficiency, performance ratio and capacity factor measure different things.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, Optimizing Solar Photovoltaic Performance for Longevity, section Understanding Solar Photovoltaic Performance, and Solar Photovoltaic Performance and Efficiency Basics, consulted 16 November 2026; International Energy Agency Photovoltaic Power Systems Programme, Reliability and Performance of Photovoltaic Systems: Best Practice Guidelines for the Use of Economic and Technical KPIs, Task 13 report, 2024, section on Performance Ratio.]

title: Solar PV Performance: Efficiency, Rated Power and Actual Energy Generation

body:
Solar thermal conversion produces heat

Solar thermal technology captures sunlight and converts it into thermal energy, or heat. Unlike a photovoltaic cell, a basic solar thermal collector does not directly generate electric current.

A solar collector generally contains a surface that absorbs incoming radiation and transfers the resulting heat to water, air or another working fluid. The heat may then be used immediately or stored for later use.

Common applications include household water heating, solar cooking, crop drying, heating water for institutions and providing heat for suitable industrial processes.

A solar thermal collector is a device that absorbs solar radiation and transfers the resulting heat to a useful medium, such as water or air.

Flat-plate solar collectors

A flat-plate collector generally contains a dark absorbing surface, passages for a heat-transfer fluid, insulation and often a transparent cover. Sunlight passes through the cover and is absorbed by the plate. The plate becomes warm and transfers heat to water or another fluid flowing through the collector.

The transparent cover and insulation help reduce heat losses. A flat-plate collector can use direct and diffuse sunlight, although the useful heat output falls when the available radiation is weak.

These collectors are widely associated with domestic and institutional hot-water systems. The heated water may be stored in an insulated tank until it is needed.

Evacuated-tube solar collectors

An evacuated-tube collector uses glass tubes containing an absorber. A vacuum within the tube structure substantially reduces heat loss through conduction and convection.

Because of their insulation, evacuated tubes can be useful where the temperature difference between the collector and surrounding air is significant. Their performance still depends on sunlight, collector design, operating conditions and maintenance.

FeatureFlat-plate collectorEvacuated-tube collector
Absorber arrangementBroad absorbing plateAbsorber enclosed within glass tubes
Heat-loss reductionInsulation and often a transparent coverVacuum insulation within the tube assembly
Common useSolar water heatingSolar water heating, including applications needing improved insulation

How solar water heating systems circulate water

Some solar water heaters use natural circulation. As water warms, its density decreases and it tends to rise. With the storage tank positioned above the collector, this movement can circulate water without an electric pump. This is known as the thermosiphon principle.

Other systems use a pump to circulate water or another heat-transfer fluid through the collector. These are called active circulation systems.

The storage tank holds heated water so that it can be used after the period of strongest sunshine. However, the stored water gradually loses heat, and prolonged cloudy conditions may require an additional heating source.

Solar cookers and solar dryers

Solar box cooker

A simple solar box cooker uses sunlight to heat food inside an insulated enclosure. A dark vessel or absorbing surface takes in radiation, while a transparent cover allows sunlight to enter and helps limit heat loss. Reflecting surfaces may direct additional sunlight into the cooker.

The food cooks because the enclosed space and vessel become hot. The cooker does not generate electricity, and it does not require a photovoltaic cell. Its cooking rate depends on available sunshine, insulation, vessel characteristics and the food being heated.

Solar dryer

A solar dryer uses heat from sunlight to increase the temperature of air or produce and assist the removal of moisture. Drying can help preserve agricultural products by lowering their moisture content. Proper airflow is important because evaporated moisture must be removed from the drying space.

Solar dryers may be used for fruits, vegetables, grains and other suitable products. Their performance depends on sunlight, ambient humidity, airflow and the properties of the material being dried.

Direct household and industrial uses

Solar thermal heat can replace part of the conventional heating requirement in homes, hostels, hospitals and industrial facilities. Suitable industrial uses include washing, drying, heating water and certain low- or medium-temperature processes.

Its important constraints are variation in sunlight, heat losses, storage capacity, suitable temperature requirements and the need for backup heat when solar energy is insufficient.

Prelims focus

  • Solar thermal collectors convert sunlight into heat rather than directly into electricity.
  • Flat-plate collectors use an absorbing plate, insulation and often a transparent cover.
  • Evacuated tubes reduce heat losses through vacuum insulation.
  • Thermosiphon circulation depends on natural movement caused by temperature-related density differences.
  • Solar cookers, water heaters and crop dryers are direct solar thermal applications.
  • Trap: A solar water heater is not necessarily a photovoltaic installation.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Mineral and Power Resources, pp. 33–34; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, p. 82; U.S. Department of Energy, Research and Development Needs for Building-Integrated Solar Technologies, sections on flat-plate collectors, evacuated-tube collectors and passive solar water heating, consulted 16 November 2026.]

title: Solar Thermal Energy: Collecting Sunlight for Heating, Cooking and Drying

body:
How concentrated solar power differs from ordinary solar heating

Concentrated solar power (CSP), also called concentrating solar thermal power, uses mirrors to collect sunlight over a comparatively large area and direct it onto a smaller receiver. The receiver absorbs the concentrated radiation and reaches a high temperature.

The thermal energy can produce steam or operate another suitable heat engine to drive a generator. CSP therefore normally follows an indirect route to electricity: sunlight is converted into heat, and heat is then converted into mechanical work and electrical energy.

A CSP mirror is not itself a photovoltaic cell. The mirror redirects sunlight; the receiver converts the concentrated radiation into heat.

The basic CSP energy pathway

  1. Collection: Mirrors intercept incoming direct sunlight.
  2. Concentration: The mirrors direct the sunlight towards a receiver.
  3. Heat absorption: A working fluid or receiver material becomes hot.
  4. Power conversion: Thermal energy drives a turbine or another heat engine connected to a generator.
  5. Electricity delivery: The generated electricity is supplied to the intended electrical system.

In many CSP plants, heat is used to produce steam that drives a turbine-generator. Dish-engine systems follow a different arrangement in which a heat engine is located near the concentrated solar receiver.

Why direct sunlight is essential for concentration

Mirrors focus light most effectively when it arrives from a well-defined direction. Direct Normal Irradiance (DNI) therefore plays a central role in assessing the solar resource for CSP.

Diffuse radiation has already been scattered in many directions and cannot be concentrated effectively by ordinary CSP mirrors. Consequently, locations with abundant strong direct sunlight, clear skies and limited cloudiness are generally better suited to conventional CSP than persistently cloudy locations.

Photovoltaic modules can use both direct and diffuse sunlight. This does not mean that PV output is unaffected by clouds; it means PV does not require the sunlight to be optically concentrated in the same manner as CSP.

Four important CSP configurations

Parabolic trough

A parabolic trough uses a long, curved mirror to focus sunlight onto a receiver tube running along the mirror's focal line. A heat-transfer fluid passing through the tube absorbs the heat. The mirror generally tracks the Sun along 1 axis.

Linear Fresnel reflector

A linear Fresnel reflector uses rows of flat or slightly curved mirrors to reflect sunlight onto an elevated linear receiver. The mirrors track the Sun to maintain the reflected light on the receiver. Like a parabolic trough, this is a line-focus arrangement.

Solar power tower

A solar power tower uses numerous sun-tracking mirrors called heliostats. They direct sunlight towards a receiver at the top of a central tower. The receiver heats a working material, which can then supply a power-generation system.

Heliostats generally track the Sun along 2 axes to keep reflected sunlight directed towards the central receiver. A tower system is a point- or central-receiver configuration rather than a line-focus system.

Parabolic dish with an engine

A parabolic dish concentrates sunlight towards a focal region near the dish, where a thermal receiver and engine-generator may be mounted. A Stirling engine is a well-known example of an engine used in dish-based systems.

Dish-engine systems are relatively modular. Unlike large conventional steam-turbine CSP plants, each dish may operate an associated engine-generator.

ConfigurationCollectorFocus or receiverTypical tracking
Parabolic troughLong curved mirrorLinear receiver tube1 axis
Linear FresnelRows of flat or slightly curved mirrorsElevated linear receiver1 axis
Solar power towerField of heliostatsCentral receiver on a tower2 axes
Parabolic dish-engineParabolic dishFocal receiver with engine2 axes

Uses beyond electricity generation

Concentrated solar heat can also be supplied directly to suitable industrial processes. Applications can include process heating, food processing, water desalination and chemical or mineral processing where the required temperature and operating pattern are suitable.

Not every CSP installation must therefore be used exclusively to generate electricity. The defining feature is the concentration of solar radiation to obtain useful heat.

Concentrated solar power and concentrated photovoltaics are different concepts. Conventional CSP concentrates sunlight to produce heat, while concentrated photovoltaic technology focuses light onto photovoltaic cells that generate electricity directly. The CSP configurations discussed here are solar thermal systems.

Prelims focus

  • CSP uses mirrors and a receiver to produce concentrated solar heat.
  • Parabolic troughs and linear Fresnel reflectors are line-focus technologies.
  • Power towers use heliostats to direct sunlight towards a central receiver.
  • Dish-engine systems concentrate sunlight near an engine-generator.
  • DNI is particularly important for CSP because conventional mirrors cannot effectively concentrate diffuse skylight.
  • Trap: Mirrors in a conventional CSP plant do not directly produce photovoltaic electricity.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, Concentrating Solar-Thermal Power Basics, Linear Concentrator System Concentrating Solar-Thermal Power Basics, Power Tower System Concentrating Solar-Thermal Power Basics and Dish/Engine System Concentrating Solar-Thermal Power Basics, consulted 16 November 2026; National Renewable Energy Laboratory, Best Practices Handbook for the Collection and Use of Solar Resource Data for Solar Energy Applications, 4th edition, September 2024, chapter 2.]
